Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 94, verses 1–4:

﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ This is an emphatic affirmation (tawqif) of the expansion of his breast (ﷺ). Its meaning is the confirmation of the expansion of his breast (ﷺ) and the enumeration of the blessings mentioned after it. The expansion of his breast (ﷺ) is its widening to acquire knowledge, and its illumination with wisdom and understanding. It is also said that it refers to Jibril's splitting of his chest in his childhood, or during the Night Journey (al-Isra') when he (ﷺ) had his heart taken out and washed.

﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾. There are three opinions concerning this. The first is the view of the majority (al-jumhur) that the burden is sins, and removing it is forgiving them. This is like His saying: ﴿that Allah may forgive you your past and future sins﴾ [al-Fath: 2]. This is according to those who permit minor sins (saghair) for the prophets, or according to the view that his sins occurred before prophethood (nubuwwah). The second is that the burden is the weights of prophethood and its obligations, and removing it means helping him to bear them and smoothing the way for his excuse after he conveyed the message (risalah). The third is that the burden is his bewilderment before prophethood, since he saw his people in error and no clear command had come to him from Allah. Removing it, according to this view, is through prophethood and guidance to the sharia (shari'ah).

﴿which had weighed down your back﴾ is an expression of the heaviness of the said burden and its severity upon him. Al-Harith al-Muhasibi said: The sins of the prophets are described as heavy, though they are minor sins that are forgiven them, because of their concern over them and their grief over them. They are heavy in their eyes because of the intensity of their fear of Allah, and light in the sight of Allah. This is like what came in a report (athar): the believer sees his sins as a mountain about to fall upon him, while the hypocrite sees his sins as a fly that passes over his nose. The derivation of "anqada zahraka" (weighed down your back) is from "naqada al-bunyan" (he broke the building) and other things, or from "al-naqid", which is the sound, as if a sound is heard from his back like the sound of something heavy being loaded upon it.

﴿And raised high your mention﴾, meaning We made your name renowned and famous in the east and the west. It is also said that it means that his mention is joined with the mention of Allah in the adhan, the khutbah, the tashahhud, and in various places in the Qur'an. A hadith has been narrated on this, that Allah said to him: "When you are mentioned, I am mentioned with you." If it is asked: why did He say "laka dhikrak" (your mention) and "laka sadrak" (your breast) when the meaning is complete without them? The answer is that His saying "laka" (for you) indicates care for him and concern for his affair.

﴿So indeed, with hardship comes ease.﴾ This is a promise of ease after hardship. He expressed it with the word *maʿa* (with), which implies closeness, to show that ease is near to hardship. If it is asked, "What is the connection between this and what precedes it?" the answer is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was in Mecca, he and his companions, in hardship from the harm of the disbelievers and from straitened circumstances, and God promised him ease. The enumeration of blessings came earlier as consolation and comfort, so that his soul would be at ease and his hope strengthened, as if He were saying: The One who bestowed these blessings upon you will help you, make you triumph, and replace this hardship with near ease. For this reason He repeated ﴿indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾ for emphasis. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "One hardship will never overcome two eases." This has been related from Umar and Ibn Mas'ud. Its interpretation (*ta'wil*) is that the hardship mentioned in this surah is one, because the definite article *al-* (the) is for previous reference, as when you say: "A man came to me, so I honored the man." The ease is two, because it is indefinite. It was also said that the first ease is in this world and the second is in the Hereafter.

﴿So when you are free, then strive.﴾ *Fa-insab* comes from *naṣb*, meaning fatigue. The meaning is: when you finish one matter, exert yourself in another. Then they differed about specifying the two matters. It was said: when you are free from the obligatory duties (*farāʾiḍ*), then exert yourself in the voluntary acts (*nawāfil*). It was said: when you are free from prayer, then exert yourself in supplication. It was also said: when you are free from the concerns of your worldly life, then exert yourself in the worship of your Lord.

﴿And to your Lord, turn with desire.﴾ He placed the prepositional phrase first to indicate exclusivity, meaning: do not turn with desire except to your Lord alone.
